sources.entry: Learning KVM - Implement Your Own Linux Kernel

summary.title: [Note] Learning KVM - implement your own kernel
summary.one_liner: You learn how to drive KVM directly via ioctl to run guest machine code, switch to 64-bit long mode with page tables, and build a tiny kernel with syscalls and hypercalls.
keywords: write a simple kernel under kvm
takeaways: KVM is driven through ioctl calls on /dev/kvm: create VM, set user memory region, create vCPU, mmap kvm_run, then loop on KVM_RUN handling exit reasons.
vCPUs start in real mode; switching to 64-bit long mode requires setting up PML4/PDPT/PDT page tables, control registers (cr0, cr3, cr4, efer) and segment registers.
Syscalls are enabled by setting EFER.SCE and registering handlers via MSRs (LSTAR, STAR, SYSCALL_MASK); the mask must be set to avoid inheriting user rflags.
Guest-to-host communication (hypercalls) can be done with out/in instructions using the port number as the hypercall ID and eax as the argument.
summary.summary: The post is a hands-on walkthrough of using the Linux KVM API directly rather than through libvirt or QEMU. It shows, with code fragments, the seven-step setup (open /dev/kvm, create VM and vCPU, map guest memory, configure registers, run and handle KVM_EXIT_HLT/KVM_EXIT_IO), then extends the guest to 64-bit long mode with page tables and segment setup. The second half covers building a minimal kernel: syscall/sysret MSR configuration, a syscall entry stub, out/in-based hypercalls to the hypervisor (e.g. a hypercall open handler), and notes on ELF loading, memory allocation, paging and user-pointer checks. The author notes the code is simplified and points to the linked kvm-kernel-example repository for working code.
